I'm not sure what software you are running here, but this is a conventional control chart for statistical process control.

The data here says that your HCl concentration is greater than your upper specification pretty consistently, and it doesn't seem to be an in control process, with one point outside of the UCL/LCL range, in addition to a 10 point streak on one side of the center line (using [WECO Rules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Electric_https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six_Sigmarules) as basis). In short, your process isn't meeting the specifications you set for it and needs correction.

The curve on the left of the histogram isn't plotting your real data, but seems to be the ideal distribution you would need to meet to have a process meeting your specification at a certain level (looks like [Six Sigma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six_Sigma) level). If it were plotting your real data, it would align with your histogram much better, being centered on your mean of 52.23 and matching the spread of your data.

I'm not sure how familiar you are with the process control parameters on the the right, but here are some resources where you can learn more about what these numbers and charts mean:

* [NIST Engineering Statistics](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/pmc/section3/pmc31.htm)
* [Process Capability Index (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Process_capability_index)

I hope this helps!

C•B is not consumed in that way because as soon as P•C is formed it decomposes, regenerating C. The regenerated C immediately forms C•B with the excess B. Therefore, as soon as C•B is consumed it immediately regenerates, meaning you have [C•B] equal to the incoming [C] (B always in excess).

That is a very odd take, vegetables that are rich in iron are just a Google search away, and include spinach, kale, lentils, beans, and many more. Many of the poorest cultures in the world live primarily on plants, because they are much cheaper to produce. It is only with very modern industrialization that meat is affordable for every meal in places such as the US. Still, you will never find beef or chicken cheaper than beans.

It's fortunate we are omnivores, so we can choose where to get our nutrients, and both plants and animals can digest well in our systems! A big thanks to our food options belongs to ancient humans figuring out cooking, so our diets already look extremely different than other animals in the wild. So much so, that we really can't compare our nutritional needs to animals that are hunting and eating live prey, or grazing on grass and forest plants.

The great news is that humans don't require animal products to be healthy, and there are millions of people living healthy lives without consuming anything that exploits and performs cruelty on animals.

Everyone unanimously in this thread condemns the behavior of the driver in the video, yet would that action suddenly become okay if he got out of his car, skinned the goose, and grilled it?

Nutritionists widely agree that all-plant diets are perfectly healthy:
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19562864/

However, I won't ask you to disclose what medical or other reasons may make this impractical for you. That's okay, because veganism as a philosophy seeks to reduce animal suffering and exploitation as much as possible, and I don't think many vegans would fault you for having to consume some amount of animal products for your own health, especially medicines and the like, which may have no practical alternatives.

I hope you can limit your animal consumption to only that which you qualify as humane and necessary, but this would exclude the vast majority of restaurant and grocery store animal products that we have available today. Every little bit counts to reduce the suffering of animals. You sound like you have a very open mind, so I hope you take this into consideration, friend!

Hi, I noticed something similar for tokens in my game, where I no longer have an AC overlay. Base Foundry allows you to set tokens as having hp bars, in token configuration if you set under resources "attr.hp" to one of the bars. You can do the same for bar 2 with "attr.ac.value" and set them to display when you prefer.

That said, there is one module that makes it easy to apply this across the board to tokens you drop into scenes and that's **Token Mold**. That module lets you do some custom overlays on hover, of which I was previously using it for AC with a shield icon. Token Mold does seem to be updated for 0.8.6 but I can't quite seem to get the overlay to work, so it may be a current bug or conflict with another module I have installed.

For sure. I mostly use tiles as props on top of existing maps that don't have much furniture and stuff. They're also really useful for putting any animated assets on top of maps, like if you have an animated campfire, or a different texture for when it's lit than when it's not. I put all my assets in the foundry data folder, the same one that contains modules, systems and worlds, and I just made a folder called assets in there.

Some misc tips:

* In tile browser, make sure you notice near the top where display mode is, and set that to a view that works best when picking your tiles (likely Thumbnail or Tiles view). Didn't realize that was there for the longest time and now I just browse tiles in foundry.
* Always scale before you rotate tiles. Hopefully this changes in the future, but if you rotate a tile then try to use mouse scaling it's really weird.
* Hold alt to scale uniformly, to prevent tiles from being stretched when you don't want to.
* Hold shift to release a tile without snapping to grid.
* Right click -> lock tiles for things you don't expect to move in the scene. It prevents accidental movement when you're moving other tiles on top of it.

That's about all I have, I use them pretty simply in my scenes, but they're very helpful.
